candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: A single concrete experience integrates moral, aesthetic, and intellectual dimensions even though explanatory thought cannot fully reconcile them, because thought is only one aspect of the experiential whole.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted answer continues the pro speaker's Bradleyan exposition from the boundary context, followed by a brief acknowledgment from the interviewer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the Bradleyan account of unified experience that underwrites the pro side's claim that intellectual or naturalistic explanation cannot exhaust reality.
candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins uses the perception of a stabbing to illustrate how evaluative feeling, aesthetic response, and physical understanding arrive together before theory separates them.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Truth is the attempted reunification of abstract, structured thought with immediate felt reality, and idealism is warranted because inquiry never intelligibly reaches outside experience itself.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same pro speaker sustains a detailed first-person exposition of Bradley's account until the interviewer's clearly marked response begins.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passage supplies the principal idealist account of truth and directly explains why correspondence with a wholly experience-independent reality is rejected.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The earlier analytic and naturalist picture treats truth as thought or language corresponding to an independently constituted world outside experience.

candidates.contextSummary: Feeling supplies detailed contact with being, thought abstracts and expands its content, and complete truth would unite both while transcending the limits of any finite perspective.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Calling reality mind-framed need not make it mind-controlled, but Bradley's appeal to an unstructured felt real risks positing a given that ordinary perception can never access without categorization.
candidates.attributionBasis: The interviewer speaks in the first person, introduces his preferred distinction, and ends with a direct question that the pro speaker subsequently answers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This grants a defensible perspectivalism while pressing a central objection to the pro account: experience appears cognitively structured from the outset.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's earlier account says immediate feeling encounters reality prior to the distinctions and abstractions imposed by reflective thought.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley distinguishes unavoidable perspectival interpretation from voluntary invention, then argues that even basic perceptual edges are learned categories that cannot simply be stripped away.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradleyan truth is constrained by operational success, action, felt encounter, and intellectual satisfaction, so idealism does not permit an arbitrarily invented but merely coherent world.
candidates.attributionBasis: The pro speaker explicitly begins answering Folley's two-part objection and develops the first answer before announcing the transition to the second question.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply protects idealism from relativism and arbitrary mind-control by supplying practical and experiential constraints on what can count as true.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley had warned that an experience-based account of truth might sound consciously controllable, merely coherent, or detached from resistant reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins invokes operational coherence to explain why false constructions fail when acted upon and presents Bradley's view as pragmatism supplemented by felt and intellectual constraints.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Reflective subjects cannot consciously recover wholly precognitive experience, yet unbounded feeling remains the foundation of thought and is ultimately integrated with complete structure, value, and agency in the absolute.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly turns to Folley's remaining question and gives a continuous Bradleyan answer until Folley introduces a comparison with Peirce.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This answers the accessibility objection while presenting the absolute as the pro side's ultimate integration of feeling, thought, goodness, and beauty.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley argued that perception is always already categorized and asked whether Bradley thinks anyone can access an entirely unstructured experiential given.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins concedes that metacognition necessarily structures experience, but says precognitive feeling persists beneath judgment and that reality's culmination unites feeling with exhaustive understanding.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: The Bradleyan absolute may function only as a Peircean regulative ideal of completed inquiry, leaving open whether it exists substantially or will ever be attained.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly frames the comparison with C. S. Peirce, contrasts possible interpretations, and asks how certain Bradley is about the absolute's existence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The challenge targets whether the pro side has justified an actually real absolute or merely redescribed inquiry's aspirational endpoint.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins had described the absolute as the endpoint where complete truth, feeling, goodness, beauty, and volition finally come together.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley compares the absolute with an ideal theory at the end of inquiry and presses whether Bradley can claim more than a useful but possibly unattainable regulative goal.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: The absolute is not merely a settled theory: complete truth must transform thought into reality itself, and the normative orientation of inquiry toward completion already recognizes that completion as more real than present partial understanding.
candidates.attributionBasis: The pro speaker labels Folley's question, states Bradley's lack of agnosticism, and gives reasons before Folley begins a practical analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the direct defense of the absolute's reality and links it to the normative intelligibility of intellectual, moral, and aesthetic striving.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley proposed that the absolute might be only a Peircean regulative ideal rather than an existent completion toward which inquiry is genuinely drawn.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins argues that thought cannot complete itself as thought alone, while every pursuit of truth presupposes and responds to a fuller reality that would satisfy it.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Purposive inquiry presupposes an attainable intelligibility, and because idealism joins knower and known rather than positing inaccessible independent being, the reality that directs inquiry cannot coherently be dismissed as fictional.
candidates.attributionBasis: After Folley's analogy, Hawkins affirms it and develops the answer continuously through a concluding claim that truth, knowledge, being, and reality converge.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passage contrasts idealism with naturalistic physicalism and argues that the practices of inquiry themselves commit us to an intelligible, experience-related reality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley asked whether belief in the absolute is an amplified version of researchers' practical assumption that intellectual, moral, or aesthetic progress is possible.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins appeals to the presuppositions of purposive search, rejects unknowable being divorced from experience, and identifies what most powerfully directs life and inquiry with reality.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: A theory is shaped by the question and aim it serves, so reductively declaring one theoretical scheme exhaustive is itself an unjustified faith commitment that excludes dimensions it cannot explain.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins answers Folley's closing question in a sustained monologue, explicitly connecting his anti-reductive conclusion to Bradley and to pragmatist insight.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This generalizes the pro critique of naturalism and scientism by arguing that every theory is purpose-relative and cannot legitimately erase resistant aspects of experience.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Earlier naturalist and analytic approaches were presented as reducing reality to what a privileged explanatory method, especially thought or science, can capture.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins uses Collingwood and the purpose-sensitive interpretation of parsimony to defend rigorous but open-ended philosophy against claims that one framework is all there is.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Anti-reductionism still requires a defensible gatekeeping standard, because inquiry must avoid both scientistic exclusion and an unrestricted free-for-all, with pragmatic consequences offering a possible middle path.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley responds directly to Hawkins's anti-reductive answer, identifies himself as unsympathetic to scientism, and states his current pragmatic preference.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This articulates the compatibilist-pragmatist alternative: methodological pluralism remains answerable to practical standards without requiring the Bradleyan absolute.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins had condemned reductive theories for denying whatever their chosen explanatory framework cannot accommodate and urged inquiry to account for everything.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley accepts the danger of excessive reduction but argues that scientism raises a legitimate demand for standards and proposes pragmatism as a difficult balance between extremes.
